routes.label: Find the vertex sectors added to the endpoint squares

question: \(ABCD\) is a square of side length \(\sqrt{3} + 1.\) Point \(P\) is on \(\overline{AC}\) such that \(AP = \sqrt{2}.\) The square region bounded by \(ABCD\) is rotated \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise with center \(P,\) sweeping out a region whose area is \(\dfrac{1}{c}(a\pi + b),\) where \(a,\) \(b,\) and \(c\) are positive integers and \(\gcd(a, b, c) = 1.\) What is \(a + b + c?\)
solution:
Take \(P\) as the origin and choose axes parallel to the square's sides. Since \(AP=\sqrt2\) lies along a square diagonal, its horizontal and vertical components both have length \(1\). Put \(r=\sqrt3\). The vertices can therefore be placed at
\[
A=(-1,-1),\quad B=(r,-1),\quad C=(r,r),\quad D=(-1,r).
\]
The initial square is \([-1,r]\times[-1,r]\). After a counterclockwise quarter-turn, it is \([-r,1]\times[-1,r]\). Their union is the rectangle
\[
R=[-r,r]\times[-1,r],
\]
whose area is \(2r(r+1)=6+2\sqrt3\).

We must also account for intermediate positions. Because \(P\) lies inside the square, every rotated square contains the full segment from \(P\) to each of its points. Fix a ray from \(P\). During the rotation, this ray samples original directions spanning \(90^\circ\). On any portion of one side of the original square, the greatest distance from \(P\) occurs at an endpoint: its squared distance has the form \(h^2+u^2\), where \(h\) is the perpendicular distance to the side and \(u\) measures displacement along it. The largest \(|u|\) on a segment occurs at an endpoint.

Consequently, the greatest distance available on the fixed ray comes either from a vertex or from an end of the sampled angular interval. Those ends correspond to the initial and final squares. This proves that the entire swept region is exactly \(R\) together with the four sectors swept by \(PA,PB,PC,PD\).

The squared vertex distances are
\[
PA^2=2,\qquad PB^2=PD^2=4,\qquad PC^2=6.
\]
Their initial directions, measured from the positive horizontal axis, are \(225^\circ,-30^\circ,120^\circ,45^\circ\), respectively. These follow from the \(45^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\)-\(60^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\) triangles in the coordinates. Each direction increases by \(90^\circ\) during the rotation. The parts of these sectors outside \(R\) are as follows.

The sector from \(PC\), spanning \(45^\circ\) to \(135^\circ\), adds a cap above \(y=r\). Its area is a quarter-circle sector of squared radius \(6\), minus the triangle with base \(2r\) and height \(r\):
\[
\frac{6\pi}{4}-\frac{(2r)r}{2}=\frac{3\pi}{2}-3.
\]
The sector from \(PA\), spanning \(225^\circ\) to \(315^\circ\), adds a cap below \(y=-1\). Its area is
\[
\frac{2\pi}{4}-\frac{2\cdot1}{2}=\frac{\pi}{2}-1.
\]
The sector from \(PB\) adds a cap to the right of \(x=r\), with endpoints \((r,-1)\) and \((r,1)\). These radii enclose \(60^\circ\), so the cap has area
\[
\frac{60}{360}\cdot4\pi-\frac{2r}{2}
=\frac{2\pi}{3}-\sqrt3.
\]
The sector from \(PD\) adds an equal cap to the left of \(x=-r\). The side caps have \(-1\le y\le1\), while the top and bottom caps stay between the rectangle's vertical sides, so these four added parts do not overlap.

Adding the rectangle and all four caps gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area}
&=6+2\sqrt3+\left(\frac{3\pi}{2}-3\right)
 +\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-1\right)\\
&\quad+2\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\sqrt3\right)\\
&=\frac{10\pi+6}{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \((a,b,c)=(10,6,3)\), whose common greatest divisor is \(1\). Therefore \(a+b+c=\boxed{19}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
